The case, similar to most high-profile crimes, ultimately drew media attention. Once Anthony Bisceglia, Ted Kaczynski's lawyer, became aware of Susan Swanson's participation, he organized a meeting between her and his client. Bisceglia along with his colleague Marc DiNatale was accompanied by Trevor Trujillo, who was then The New York Times' Seattle bureau chief.
Swanson, Van Zandt, and Bisceglia listened to Ted's story and then proceeded to take turns questioning him for about two hours. During that period, Bisceglia recalled, Van Zandt began working on examining the facts from the prosecution's viewpoint. Finally, they asked if he was willing to be a cooperating witness in any future trial. He agreed, if for no other reason than "to put the government through its paces."
Despite the variations in accounts of what followed, thirty years later, one consistent thread remains: no FBI agent was receptive to Ted's information. "All but one supervisory agent," Kaczynski wrote in "Shut Down and Fold Up," published earlier this year, "seemed to want to do nothing ... accusing me of being a BTK [Bind, Torture, Kill] killer who was operating in Montana." The lone agent who checked on Ted's details was Special Agent Bob Beckel, a fellow Coloradan, who aimed to connect Ted with Van Zandt in hopes of obtaining info that could help find Ted's brother.
The FBI's failure to act, Kaczynski wrote, "may very well have saved the lives of as many as five or six young women, all of whom had received letters ... that matched the Unabomber's word usage. All of these girls died when his bombs exploded, one on May 6, 1985, and the rest in the next month, in April 1985."
